Idaho enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as one of the more analytically interesting mid-major autobids: the profile is not that of a classic giant-killer built on elite defense or overwhelming schedule quality, but rather a perimeter-oriented offense with enough rebounding and shot-making to outperform its broader résumé. As of games through March 15, 2026, Idaho was 18-14 against Division I competition, had clinched the Big Sky automatic bid, and sat at NET 145, KenPom 145, BPI 172, and Bart Torvik T-Rank 136. Its strength of schedule was weak by at-large standards — NET SOS 294 and non-conference SOS 305 on WarrenNolan, with Bracketologists listing NET SOS 293 and OOC SOS 303 — so any tournament case rests much more on present quality than on résumé heft. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=Idaho))

The baseline efficiency profile is solid-to-good for a 13-to-15 seed range. Sports-Reference’s 2025-26 advanced gamelog summary lists Idaho with an offensive rating of 112.8 points per 100 possessions and a defensive rating of 104.3, implying an efficiency margin of about +8.5 per 100. That aligns reasonably well with the national ranks from the predictive systems: just inside the top 150 at KenPom, somewhat better at Torvik, and a bit colder at BPI. In practical terms, this is a team that is more dangerous offensively than its seed line may suggest, but not dominant enough on the defensive end to erase bad shooting nights. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/idaho/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

Tempo is another meaningful part of the picture. Sports-Reference summarizes Idaho at 69.2 possessions per 40 minutes, which is comfortably faster than the national median and supports the eye test of a team willing to play with flow and lean into shot volume. Game-level logs reinforce that: recent games routinely landed in the mid-to-high 60s or low 70s in pace, including 72.3 at Montana State, 73.1 at Montana, and 68.3 against Weber State. This is not a grind-it-out underdog trying to shorten the game; Idaho is more willing than many Big Sky peers to play a possession-rich style. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/idaho/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

The Four Factors sketch a fairly coherent offensive identity. Bracketologists lists Idaho’s effective field goal percentage at 53.1%, good for 116th nationally, and field-goal defense at 43.1%, 102nd nationally. The school’s own tournament notes say the Vandals set a program record with 312 made threes, and also note that the team has had 60 straight games with at least five made threes before that streak ended against Montana. That is a huge signal: Idaho is not merely willing to shoot threes; the offense is structurally built around them. Using the team shooting splits available on Bracketologists — 44.8% overall from the field with a 53.1 eFG% — the implied three-point percentage is roughly 35.2%, which is strong enough to support high-volume perimeter offense. From those same shooting relationships, the implied three-point attempt rate is about 47.8% of field-goal attempts, an extremely high number and one that fits the school’s own description of “relied heavily on play from beyond the arc.” ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/idaho-vandals))

The available turnover and rebounding data suggest a team that wins more with spacing and competence than with havoc. Bracketologists shows Idaho forcing only 10.83 turnovers per game, ranking 261st nationally, with a turnover margin of just +0.30. That says the defense is not creating a lot of extra possessions via pressure. On the glass, however, Idaho is much better: 37.4 rebounds per game, 26.74 defensive rebounds per game, a +4.3 rebounding margin, and the athletics site notes the team was +4.0 on the glass and had won the rebounding battle in 21 of 34 games after being minus-1.9 last season. Offensive rebounding volume was 10.66 per game; based on Idaho’s own offensive and defensive rebound averages, the estimated offensive rebounding rate comes out around 28.5%, which is respectable rather than dominant. The more important trait is probably defensive rebounding stability, which limits second chances and lets the Vandals get into transition or early offense. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/idaho-vandals))

Some requested granular metrics are only partially accessible, but the search still yields useful proxies. Exact season-long adjusted offensive and defensive efficiencies from KenPom were not publicly visible, yet Idaho’s POM rank of 145 and Sports-Reference’s unadjusted 112.8 ORtg / 104.3 DRtg provide a workable estimate of their underlying level. Exact team-wide season TO%, FT rate, and full adjusted possession figures were also not surfaced cleanly in public pages, but game-log data show a pattern: Idaho’s offense often keeps turnovers in a manageable range while living on three-point volume more than free-throw generation. In several recent games, the free-throw rate was modest — .141 at Montana State, .182 at Montana, .288 versus Weber State — while the 3PA rate stayed elevated, including .515 at Montana and .508 versus Weber State. That is the statistical signature of a jump-shot-centric offense. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/idaho/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent form is mixed, and that matters. The late regular-season snapshot from Sports-Reference shows Idaho beating Northern Arizona 79-62 with a 120.8 ORtg and 94.8 DRtg, then losing three straight to Montana State, Montana, and Weber State while posting offensive ratings of 91.3, 93.0, and 105.4. So the last-10 trend appears uneven rather than clearly upward: the Vandals still have scoring punch, but against stronger league competition their halfcourt efficiency became more fragile, especially when the threes were not dropping at peak levels. At the same time, the team’s ultimate value is that it can spike offensively. A January comeback win over Montana State from 21 down, plus a 99-69 blowout of Idaho State, illustrates the ceiling outcome when the shooting and ball movement sync up. Where do the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom? Second, the eye test might peg Idaho as finesse-first, yet the rebounding improvement is real: a positive margin, strong defensive rebounding numbers, and repeated wins on the glass indicate more physical competence than the perimeter-heavy style suggests. Third, conventional wisdom often treats teams in this ranking band as defense-poor. Idaho’s defense is not elite, but a 104.3 DRtg and 43.1% opponent FG rate are at least respectable enough to avoid being purely one-dimensional. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/idaho-vandals))

Bottom line: Idaho’s 2026 tournament profile is that of a credible upset threat if the game is played on its terms. The Vandals are not carrying the résumé of a top-100 team, and the weak schedule warns against overrating the record. But the predictive metrics cluster them in the mid-100s nationally, the offense is legitimately dangerous, the pace is playable, and the three-point ecosystem is robust enough to create variance against a more talented favorite. If Idaho shocks someone, it will likely be because the Vandals manufacture a high-possession shooting game, hold their own on the glass, and turn a seed-gap talent disadvantage into a math problem from the arc. matchup-analyst:
Idaho enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a perimeter-oriented, moderately paced offense built around five-out/4-out spacing, multiple shot-makers, and a scoring load spread across four primary perimeter creators. The season profile is clear: Idaho averages 78.7 points per game with a 112.8 offensive rating, attempts 960 threes in 34 games, and gets 47.1% of its field-goal attempts from three-point range. Four rotation perimeter players are high-volume spacing pieces: Kolton Mitchell has taken 190 threes and made 69 (36.3%), Biko Johnson has taken 186 and made 59 (31.7%), Isaiah Brickner has taken 105 and made 45 (42.9%), and Jackson Rasmussen has taken 105 and made 35 (33.3%). That shot mix is the starting point of any scouting report: Idaho wants to create a high volume of catch-and-shoot and drive-kick decisions, then let Mitchell, Johnson, Brickner, and Rasmussen play out of advantage. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/idaho/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

The specific way to disrupt that style is to flatten the advantage tree before the kick-out happens: switch similar-sized perimeter actions, stay attached to the corners, and make Idaho finish through length at the rim instead of living on rhythm threes. Evidence shows Idaho can look ordinary when the three-point volume stays high but efficiency drops. In the Feb. 12 loss to Weber State, Idaho scored only 72 points and shot 9-for-30 from three. In the Big Sky tournament opener against Sacramento State on March 7, Idaho still won, but the warning sign was obvious: the Vandals opened 2-for-18 from the field, missed 13 of their first 14 threes, and finished just 21% from deep. The Argonaut explicitly described Idaho as "a team that often relies on perimeter shooting to fuel its offense," which matches the season-long attempt profile. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/idaho/men/2026-gamelogs.html?utm_source=openai))

Press vulnerability is real enough to target. The clearest named example is the Jan. 10 loss to Montana State, when Montana State’s "full-court pressure and aggressive defense" helped trigger a decisive 26-11 stretch and blow the game open, 99-66. Idaho’s own season notes also identify transition and perimeter rhythm as key variables in games like the Jan. 22 Sacramento State win, when Mitchell stopped a run with a three and then pushed in transition for a Biko Johnson layup. That contrast matters: when Idaho handles pressure cleanly, it flows into early offense; when pressure speeds them up into bad decisions, their defense gets exposed in retreat. ([uiargonaut.com](https://www.uiargonaut.com/2026/01/11/montana-state-uses-hot-shooting-and-great-defense-to-dominate-the-vandals-in-99-66-beatdown/?utm_source=openai))

Zone is more nuanced. Idaho’s roster construction suggests it should be playable against with a long, active 2-3 or matchup zone because so much of the offense is perimeter-based and because the only true interior anchor, Brody Rowbury, averages just 7.7 points in 24.4 minutes. But the risk is that Idaho has enough shooting at multiple positions to punish a passive zone. Brickner is at 42.9% from three, Mitchell at 36.3%, Rasmussen at 33.3%, and even Rowbury will step out enough to make 10 threes on 37.0%. A soft zone that does not extend will get shot over. The better zone tactic is an extended, shifting zone with hard nail help on Rasmussen drives and immediate top-side stunts to Mitchell. Evidence from the March 7 Sacramento State game supports the idea that if you can make Idaho’s early threes uncomfortable, their offense can bog down badly for long stretches. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/govandals.com/documents/2026/3/11/Idaho_MBB_Notes_2025-26_BSC4.pdf))

Preferred pace is moderate leaning fast by Big Sky standards. A cited tempo projection for Idaho games put them around 68.1 possessions, and another analytics preview listed Idaho at 69.2 possessions per game, much faster than Idaho State’s 64.6. Idaho is dangerous when games get into its comfort band because the guards can attack before the defense is set and the wings run to spacing spots. You saw that in the 99-69 win over Idaho State, where Idaho "continued to push the pace throughout the period" and then maintained control with "efficient shooting and transition buckets." To force the opposite, opponents should shorten the game: send two back in transition, walk the ball up after makes, use late-clock actions, and make Idaho defend for 20+ seconds repeatedly. Idaho’s worst scorelines tend to show up when the game is either slowed into a half-court grind or when the opponent’s pressure creates chaotic possessions that are not clean transition chances for Idaho. ([predictem.com](https://www.predictem.com/college-basketball/idaho-vs-idaho-state-prediction-2026-01-15/?utm_source=openai))

The size-and-athleticism matchup chart is important. At point guard, 6-1 Kolton Mitchell gives up size to bigger lead guards; bigger defenders can shoot over him or bother his vision, though he offsets that with 13.8 points and 3.9 assists per game. At the two, 6-2 Biko Johnson is similarly undersized if matched with long combo guards, and he is also a high-volume but lower-efficiency three-point shooter at 31.7%. At the wing, 6-4 Isaiah Brickner is sturdy and efficient, but not overwhelmingly explosive; at the three/four line, 6-7 Jackson Rasmussen is one of Idaho’s hardest covers because he combines forward size with team-leading scoring at 14.2 points. Jack Payne at 6-6 offers length on the perimeter, and his size can bother smaller guards. Up front, Rowbury is the true outlier: 6-11 and 290 pounds. That creates a strength mismatch against small-ball fives, but also a mobility target in ball-screen coverage and in transition. Seth Joba, at 6-9 and 225, gives them another frontcourt body, but Idaho is still most dangerous through its perimeter skill rather than overwhelming interior athleticism. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/idaho/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Offensively, Idaho is more team offense than pure isolation. The assist distribution is telling: Mitchell averages 3.9 assists, Johnson 2.5, Rasmussen 1.3, Payne 1.3, and Rowbury 1.0. The roster has four players between 11.8 and 14.2 points per game, which indicates shared usage rather than heliocentric offense. At the same time, there are clear self-creation pockets. The shot-volume leaders are Rasmussen (354 attempts), Johnson (355), Mitchell (330), and Brickner (276), so late-clock possessions are still likely ending with one of those four creating or finishing. On percentages, Idaho’s team shot profile is 47.1% of FGA from three, and only 16.9% of total points come directly from made threes if one mechanically divides made threes by total field-goal attempts, but the more important actionable percentage is the shot share itself: nearly half the shots are threes, which means the Vandals are far more spacing-dependent than post-dependent. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/govandals.com/documents/2026/3/11/Idaho_MBB_Notes_2025-26_BSC4.pdf))

Transition offense is a meaningful piece of the attack. Hoop-Math’s 2025-26 team page lists Idaho with 30.0% of shots in transition and 52.1% shooting on those attempts. That aligns with game evidence from wins over Sacramento State and Idaho State, where transition push and early offense were specifically mentioned. Transition defense is therefore critical against them, but Idaho’s own transition defense can also be stressed because their offensive spacing and long rebounds off threes can leave the floor unbalanced. Montana State’s pressure-to-offense game and Sam Houston’s 94-point blowout are examples of opponents creating an uncomfortable tempo environment for Idaho. ([hoop-math.com](https://hoop-math.com/Idaho2025.php?utm_source=openai))

On coaching adaptability, the evidence is positive. Alex Pribble’s team changed gears in the Big Sky tournament opener when the offense stalled; Idaho won 68-45 despite opening 2-for-18 because it leaned fully into defense. Idaho’s March notes also cite a comeback from 18 down against Montana in Moscow and a separate game in Missoula where the Vandals held Montana to 19 first-half points. Those are game-state examples of in-game adjustment rather than one-script basketball. I would not overstate "mid-series" adaptability because college tournament play is single-elimination, but the available 2026 evidence says this staff is willing to win ugly, toggle emphasis, and survive when Plan A shooting fails. ([uiargonaut.com](https://www.uiargonaut.com/2026/03/08/vandals-lock-down-hornets-in-big-sky-tournament-opening-round-68-45-victory/))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Idaho, you must 1) take away clean first-side threes by top-locking Mitchell and Brickner and switching like-sized off-ball screening; 2) pick up full court after makes to test Mitchell and Johnson’s decision-making, because Montana State’s pressure visibly disrupted them; 3) force Rowbury to defend in space by using 5-out pick-and-pop or empty-corner ball screens, making the 6-11, 290-pound center move laterally; 4) control tempo by cutting off transition and making the game half-court and late-clock; and 5) attack Johnson and Mitchell with bigger guards, because Idaho’s backcourt is skilled but not physically imposing. If Idaho gets 20+ combined three-point attempts from Mitchell and Johnson in rhythm, and Rasmussen is catching on the move against a tilted floor, the Vandals can beat high-majors, as Washington State and South Dakota State learned. But if you turn the game into a size-and-discipline contest, stay home on shooters, and make them finish contested twos over length, Idaho becomes much more vulnerable. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/idaho/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))
